title: Illness and the homeopathic doctor
summary: A doctor uses psychology and hospital visits to help him.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: And what have you done since?

Well, there wasn't -- I couldn't go anywhere, I was a sick man. I was a sick man. And I told you, I went to specialist after specialist, and all I money went for doctors' medicine, doctors' -- there was that one man who said he could cure me, he was a homeopathic doctor. And he did me a lot of good, and he told me, well, he got one arm up so I could raise it. He was working on this one when he died.

Now, the kind of medicine he gave me, I do not know what it was. It was his own, he got his own medicine. But had he lived, he would have cured me entirely. He said he would. He said, it'll take time, Scotty. It'll take time. You got to do exactly like I want. He was a good man, too, and when you have faith in your doctor, you can heal with him, because you work with your doctor. If you don't like your doctor, there ain't no sense going to him, because you're not going to get well.

He was very nice to me and I liked him. He used to take me around with him to visit. I'd be going along the avenue sometimes and I'd hear somebody -- hey, Scottie, I'd look around and hear, come here, come here. (Unintelligible.)
I'd say, Doctor, I got to go on and (unintelligible), and he'd say, never mind that, tell them you're with me. Come on, I want to show you something.

Well, I had to hop in, he's my doctor now, so I knew I'd be safe with him. He'd take me around to different hospitals, have me to go up and visit patients with him. And I wasn't no doctor. But, you see, he was smart. He wanted to show me people that were worse off than I was.

And how they were recuperating. And he'd go in there, and he'd tell jokes. He had a joke for everybody, make them laugh. Man would be laying there with one arm all bandaged up and one leg up in the air and all, and he'd make the man laugh.

Now, afterwards, it came to me. He called me and took me over to St. Luke's Hospital. When he told me to go with him, I used common sense. He was my doctor. And as long as I was with him, I wouldn't do anything wrong. So and Jean, she understood, too. She had had a private talk with him while I was home one day. She went up there to get me some medicine. And she understood. So long as I was with Doc, I was all right.

He took me to St. Luke's and on the way, I said, Doctor, did you ever study psychology? It came to me. He put it off, he says, oh, yes, yes, I took it for awhile, but I gave it up, it cost too much money. See, that's what he'd been using on me, psychology, yeah. He was trying to get my thoughts away from my illness, that there were plenty of people worse off than me. And I forgot about it, because I was worried to death I couldn't play.
He told me, no, no, you can't play, how could you? And he was telling the truth. I couldn't hold my arm up like that and blow. Gosh.
